name: Giovanni Boccaccio
credit: Giovanni Boccaccio, fresco by Andrea del Castagno (c. 1450, Uffizi, Florence) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375) was a Florentine writer, born in or near Certaldo and raised in Florence. Sent to Naples as a young man to train in commerce and then canon law, he found instead the court and learned circle of King Robert of Anjou, where he began to write in Latin and in the Tuscan vernacular. The Decameron, his collection of one hundred tales told during the plague of 1348, is the work that made his name.

Besides the Decameron, Boccaccio wrote the romance Filocolo, the epic Teseida, the pastoral Ninfale fiesolano and the Elegia di Madonna Fiammetta, as well as Latin works on mythology and famous men and women, and a life of Dante, whose Commedia he publicly expounded in Florence. He was a friend and admirer of Petrarch. Il Filostrato, an early narrative poem in ottava rima on the love of Troilo and Griseida, is the source of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde.
